title: April 2022: 3D Character Sheets
body:
Our tabletop games are increasingly 3D. We have 3D VTTs with 3D animated maps, 3D printed miniatures, and of course we roll 3D dice. But we're still using the same flat old 2D character sheets we've had since the 1970s!
It's time for that to change. Dyslexic Character Sheets is proud to give you a special preview of the first ever 3D character sheet...

title: Edit and Save is live!
body:
After more than a year working on it, I've finally released some massive new features:
- Edit all the fields in the character sheet, including proficiencies, alignment, etc.
- Calculations work automatically (*)
- Save your character sheet
These features are for patrons only. You'll need to subscribe (at the $1 minimum rate) and log in using your Patreon account to get the benefits.
Full editing has been the #1 requested feature in all the years I've been building these. It was only made possible because of the way the new Pathfinder 2e sheets are built - which, sadly, means it doesn't apply the Pathfinder 1e, Starfinder or D&D 3.5e character sheets.
While these new features are only for patrons, the character sheets themselves are as free as they always have been. Accessibility features and translations are also free. For a breakdown of exactly what's free and what's reserved, see the Patrons page.
(*) Not all the classes and archetypes are fully calculated yet, but most of them should be.

title: Some thoughts on One D&D and the OGL
body:
I've seen rumours that One D&D won't be getting a OGL.
If you're not familiar with it, the Open Game License is a legal document that permits anybody to use the D&D rules in their own publications provided they respect their intellectual property. It's what allows third-party publishers to make adventures and other content for the game, it's what allows games like Pathfinder to exist, and it's what allows me to make character sheets legally.
The openness of the game has spawned a great deal of the creativity that's blossomed in the RPG space. Without it, D&D would not be the commercial success it is now.
It sounds like WotC sees all this money going to other people and want to get that for themselves. The move into the digital space, with the purchase of D&D Beyond and the development of their own VTT, indicates that they want to own the whole D&D experience. If true, this is a short-sighted decision, both for WotC and for the hobby as a whole.
I have no insider information. I don't know if this rumour is true.
But I do know that, without a legal framework, I could not make character sheets for it. Nor would I want to.

title: On the OGL
body: You've probably seen this already: Dungeons & Dragons’ New License Tightens Its Grip on Competition. I was waiting to see what One D&D looked like before deciding whether to make character sheets for it. Well, if there's any truth at all to these reports (and they look pretty solid), then I won't be going anywhere near it.

title: A year on
body:
It's a year now since the OGL crisis hit.
It's hard to explain just how deeply it affected everyone who creates things for TTRPGs. Just how worried, angry and betrayed it made us feel.
D&D is more than just a property that a company can own. It's a folk game, and a whole community and identity built around it. It's the product of countless people, some of them working for the hundreds of publishers, or the thousands of part-time creators, but most of all it's the many players and DMs who've made this game what it is.
It seems obscene that a profit-seeking company could have control over it, and more so that they could choose to take the whole thing away.
That nightmare was averted this time, due to the speed and scale of our reaction. Executives honestly didn't expect the reaction they got - because they don't actually know anything about the players or community. Just think on that. This catastrophic course of action was taken by people who don't care enough to get to know the people it affects.
And it wasn't even smart greed. I'm used to greed - I live in capitalism the same as the rest of you. It was incompetent, self-defeating greed, that wouldn't even have served their business interests even if it had worked entirely according to plan. And those idiots are getting million-dollar bonuses now.
I'm not going to replay the events of the crisis blow-by-blow. I expect you'll see plenty of that in the next few days. I just want you to remember why it mattered.

title: AI
body:
Two years ago, I made a joke post about how Dyslexic Character Sheets would not be using NFCs or cryptocurrencies. Since then crypto has largely been forgotten as the dumb fad it always was - there's a few losers still burning their graphics cards mining it, but nobody cares about them.
The new hotness now is AI. But this one isn't as funny.
The camera has always lied. People have always used the semblance of reality offered by photography to tell their own version of the story. Stalin was using airbrushed photos back in the 1930s, and political leaders around the world have followed. Photoshop has continually made it easier to fake reality. Visual effects that were once the reserve of billion dollar companies are now in the hands of every amateur with a decent graphics card.
But the possibilities offered by AI-generated video now blow all that out of the water. What they can do is incredible - and terrifying.
It's reaching the point where ANY real world evidence you see - whether that's a photograph, an interview with a world leader, or live footage of an event - could be fake.
It snuck up on us. A year ago we were laughing at how they couldn't get the number of fingers right. Then they got better, and cheaper, and they'll keep getting better and cheaper until anyone can do anything.
A few weeks ago we heard about an employee in a Hong Kong office who was persuaded to transfer $25m to criminals by a faked live video call with his boss. A lot of us work from home nowadays, or work internationally over video, or travel and work remotely. How many of us would be able to look at our boss's face on a live video call and say, "I don't think you're real"?
It's election season in the US, and that means lies. We've seen faked videos of Biden saying things he never actually said. And these are early days - in 4 or 8 years the techniques will be so much more powerful. Voters won't be able to tell what's real any more.
Compared to those costs, I don't see any benefit from the existence of these things. But the genie won't go back into the bottle now.

title: Paizo Community Use Policy
body:
There's been a change in Paizo's licenses. The Community Use Policy has been removed, and a new Fan Content Policy added in its place.
The Community Use Policy was useful for granting access to the Pathfinder and Starfinder logos. The Fan Content Policy explicity doesn't cover projects like this one, so I think I can no longer use them. I'm still trying to understand how the Compatibility License fits into this.
Short version, I probably won't be able to use a lot of Paizo's artwork in the future.

title: D&D 5.5
body:
As I'm sure you're aware from all the publicity, the first of the new D&D books (2024 revision? 5.5? 5.2? 5.24?) come out soon.
I have strong reasons for continuing to boycott Hasbro, reasons that are no less valid than they were 18 months ago. A company that refuses to understand its community, tries to sabotage a whole market sector, mistreats its workers, and sacks many of the greatest names in the industry while giving its executives and shareholders big fat bonuses, does not deserve to be the steward of the game we love.
That said, I understand that D&D is the social glue that many of us rely on. Not everyone has the luxury of a group who'll move onto another game with us, and refusing to play it can be like refusing to drink at the same bar as all your friends. For all the talk of compatibility, the power creep in the new edition means that playing an older character at a table with newer ones is likely to be frustrating. So I don't judge anybody who feels they need to get them.
Meanwhile, the problem with Paizo's license changes is serious, and isn't resolved yet. Expect a long post about that when I'm less covidy.

title: Sigil VTT is dead
body:
Sigil VTT is dead.
<shocked pikachu>
Anybody who knows either the TTRPG business, or the videogame business, could have told them just how ambitious a project it is, how much it would cost, how difficult it would be to make space in the crowded VTT market, and how short a shelf life it would have compared to the half-century D&D has been around.
I don't know exactly how much money Hasbro poured down this drain, but it's going to be millions. If they had 30+ developers working on this for at least 3 years, that's a minimum of $10 million, and probably multiple times that.
It was never going to recoup even a fraction of those millions, even in the most successful scenarios. It could have been a slow, moderate success; but in a desperate effort to make it pay back quickly, Hasbro would have hit the microtransactions button too hard and burned the market. As it is, they won't even get that.
This is all very predictable. They should, and could, have seen this coming a mile away and saved themselves the pain. But Hasbro are a bad company.
https://gizmodo.com/dnd-sigil-vtt-canceled-hasbro-wizards-of-the-coast-2000578128
